why_them: Six of our twenty Amsterdam trees stand in their garden, including the cycad in the Palmenkas that is one of the oldest potted plants in the world, plus the Turkish hazel, the twisted catalpa, the shellbark hickory, the Turner's oak and the ginkgo.
Four of Leiden's six trees are theirs: the tulip tree planted in Boerhaave's time, the ginkgo, the weeping beech by the pond and the golden chain near the entrance.
The national register of monumental trees they keep overlaps directly with the thirteen Dutch cities we publish, and they are the obvious party to check whether our ages and pins hold up.
Three of Utrecht's five trees stand in their Oude Hortus: the ginkgo, the handkerchief tree and the yew.

org: Stichting tot instandhouding van de begraafplaats Groenesteeg Leiden
why_them: The Groenesteeg beech on our Leiden page stands on the cemetery this volunteer foundation restored and maintains, and they are the only people who know its planting history.
The summer linden near the Sterckshof in their park is one of our ten Antwerp trees, and the estate's own gardeners hold its measurement history.

Rotterdam's own arboretum, three kilometres from the Park plane and the Westersingel planes we publish, and the single best-placed party in the city to correct a species or an age on our Rotterdam page.
Two of Baarn's five trees stand on their Groeneveld estate: the tulip tree grove by the ijskelder and the copper beech at the south pond.
The dawn redwood and the giant sequoia in their former Utrecht University botanical garden are two of our five Baarn trees, and we have no photograph of either.
Three of Arnhem's four trees are on their estate: De Poortwachters at the Zijpendaal entrance and the Dalweg oak in Gulden Bodem.
The juttepeer in the courtyard of the Heilige Geesthofje on the Paviljoensgracht is the opening tree of our Hague page and one of the oldest pear trees in the country.
blocked_reason: Wrong target: haagsehofjes.nl is a biscuit company (Rogier Dop, reply 2026-08-16), not the foundation behind the Heilige Geesthofje. The juttepeer still needs the hofje itself or the Haags Hofjesberaad; no verified address yet.

why_them: They publish their own Hague tree walks, and our five Hague trees (Koekamp oak, Clingendael linden, Postzegelboom, Kabouterboom) overlap with the trees they campaign for.
The mulberries in their own courtyard on the Molenstraat are the first entry on our Breda page.

Three of Den Bosch's four trees grow on the city wall itself: the weichselboom on the Parklaan, the Norway maple on Bastion Oranje and the trio on Bastion Vught, which is exactly the fortification they guide people around.
The cut-leaved horse chestnut in Park Middelheim and the park trees of Kasteel Den Brandt next door are two of our ten Antwerp entries.
The Flemish tree-care association whose members manage the very parks our Antwerp and Brussels pages send people to, including Rivierenhof and the Parc d'Egmont group of six.

Flanders' forest organisation, and our Brussels page publishes sixteen trees including the Bois de la Cambre pond oaks and the Hippodrome douglas fir on the edge of the Sonian Forest they campaign for.
The black mulberry of the Jardin Botanique on the Rue Royale is one of our sixteen Brussels trees and we have no photograph of it.

They manage most of the parks our sixteen Brussels trees stand in, from Parc Tournay-Solvay and the Bois de la Cambre to the Parc de Woluwe sequoia, and they keep the regional remarkable-tree inventory.
Flanders' largest nature association, with local afdelingen in Antwerp and Brussels where our twenty-six Belgian trees stand.

They work directly with Flemish municipal green services, which is exactly who would know whether the Peace Tree on Antwerp's Grote Markt and the Millennium Ginkgo of the Stadspark are described correctly on our page.
Their local afdelingen walk the exact parks we publish, and they are the natural route to a member who could photograph the trees we still have no image of.
They already run guided walks along monumental trees in Dutch cities, which is the same walk our thirteen Dutch city pages describe.
Three of our Amsterdam trees are inside their gates: the Heimanseik, the Persian ironwood and the coast redwood, and the Heimanseik is the tree we open the Amsterdam page with.
They fight tree by tree for Utrecht's canopy, and our Utrecht page publishes the Uithof linden, the three Oude Hortus trees and the Onder de Linden row on the Nieuwegracht.
Four of our five Groningen trees are theirs to watch: the star point oaks and winter oak of the Sterrebos, the duck's foot tree in the Noorderplantsoen and the Groenestein plane.
Amsterdam is our deepest Dutch city at twenty trees, including the Olifantsiep on the Zeeburgerdijk and the Lomanstraat tunnel of planes, both of which they have campaigned about.
The Leidsebosje planes and the Amstelveld wingnuts on our Amsterdam page are exactly the kind of city-centre veterans they track.
Leiden is their region, and two of our six Leiden trees stand outside the Hortus: the Beets beech on the Burcht mound and the Groenesteeg cemetery beech.
Our four Haarlem trees are all in their patch: the Lodewijk Napoleon beech in the Haarlemmerhout, the Provinciehuis plane in the Griffietuin, the Kleverlaan yew and the Kenaupark red beech.
They keep their own page on Rotterdam's monumental trees, which covers the Park plane by the Euromast and the Westersingel planes we publish. No address is printed on their site, only a form.

They manage estates on the edge of several cities we publish, including the Sint-Pietersberg side of Maastricht where our 1700 Oaks of the Cannerbos stand. Their site publishes only a form and a privacy address.
The historic grounds of the zoo beside Antwerpen-Centraal are one of our ten Antwerp entries and the oldest planted ground in the city centre. Their site publishes a form only.
They publish a Dutch and Flemish guide to bijzondere bomen with stories, photos and locations, the closest thing to a peer we have in Dutch, and the most likely site to link to a city page.
A Dutch blog that writes regularly about remarkable trees, and a natural place for a piece on the twenty Amsterdam trees we publish.
A Flemish walking blog, and our Brussels page is a walk: six of the sixteen trees stand together in the Parc d'Egmont, which is a fifteen-minute loop off the Sablon.

why_them: Vrienden van Sonsbeek named them as the desk with the tree expertise in Arnhem, which makes this a warm approach rather than a cold one. Our four Arnhem trees include De Poortwachters at the Zijpendaal entrance and the Dalweg oak, and three of the four have no photograph.
